children.topic: I. Definition
Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow tract — from small intrahepatic venules to suprahepatic IVC [7][8]
Rare: 0.5–2 per million (Western); 5–7 per million (Asia) [7]
II. Etiology / Risk Factors
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) — ~50% of cases; screen with JAK2 V617F mutation [7][9]
Prothrombotic states identified in 79–84% of patients; ≥2 disorders in 25–46% [7]
Inherited: Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency [9][8]
Acquired: antiphospholipid syndrome, PNH, OCPs, pregnancy [10][8]
Systemic: Behçet disease, sarcoidosis, vasculitis [9]
Secondary (non-thrombotic): malignant invasion/compression of hepatic veins [7]
III. Pathophysiology
Hepatic venous obstruction → ↑ sinusoidal pressure → centrilobular congestion and ischemia [8][11]
Ischemic injury → free radical release → hepatocyte necrosis (centrilobular) [8]
Chronic congestion → sinusoidal thrombosis → centrilobular fibrosis → cirrhosis [9][11]
Caudate lobe hypertrophy — independent drainage directly into IVC [8]
Compensatory: intrahepatic collaterals + increased arterial flow [11]
IV. Clinical Presentation
Classic triad: abdominal pain + hepatomegaly + ascites [12][7]
~20% asymptomatic (chronic, with collateral formation) [12][7]
Subacute = most common presentation [10][7]
Fulminant: acute liver failure with encephalopathy
Chronic: portal hypertension complications, risk of HCC [10]
V. Diagnostic Workup
Doppler ultrasound — first-line; absent/reversed hepatic vein flow [7]
CT/MRI: patchy liver enhancement, caudate lobe hypertrophy, venous collaterals [7]
Venography: "spider web" pattern of collaterals [8]
Liver biopsy: only if small-vessel BCS suspected [9]
Always screen for MPN (JAK2 V617F) even if another cause found [9][12]
Full thrombophilia workup in all patients [7]
VI. Management Stepwise Approach
Step 1: Anticoagulation (LMWH → warfarin) — lifelong in most patients [10]
Step 2: Angioplasty ± stenting of stenotic hepatic veins/IVC [9][13]
Step 3: TIPS — for refractory cases or deteriorating liver function [9][12]
Step 4: Liver transplantation — definitive for end-stage/fulminant cases [10][9]
Treat underlying prothrombotic condition (e.g., cytoreduction for MPN)
5-year survival with stepwise strategy: ~90% [9]
VII. Complications
Progressive cirrhosis and portal hypertension
Hepatocellular carcinoma — mechanism linked to hyperarterialization rather than chronic inflammation [11]
Portal vein thrombosis (concurrent in many cases) [14][8]
Focal nodular hyperplasia-like nodules [7][14]
VIII. Key Pearls / Connections
Suspect BCS in any unexplained acute/chronic liver disease — especially young patients with ascites [13]
Discovery of one prothrombotic factor should not stop further workup — multiple causes common [9]
JAK2 V617F testing essential even if another etiology identified [9]
Pregnancy not contraindicated post-BCS, but fetal outcomes remain poor [10]
Cirrhosis ↔ Budd-Chiari
Chronic BCS causes a unique veno-centric cirrhosis pattern distinct from viral/alcoholic cirrhosis; conversely, pre-existing cirrhosis is a risk factor for BCS [9][14]
Portal hypertension is the shared final common pathway — but mechanisms differ (intrahepatic resistance in cirrhosis vs. post-sinusoidal congestion in BCS)
Differential trap: Cryptogenic cirrhosis — always consider chronic BCS as an overlooked cause, especially with prominent caudate hypertrophy or IVC compression on imaging [15]
